2. On your retargeting and post-view audiences, lean hard into the story the competitor can't tell — sourcing, wax quality, burn time. Cold buyers compare price; warm buyers compare story.

3. Quietly raise prices on 2-3 SKUs by ~8-10%. Counterintuitive but specifically tested: when a cheap clone appears, raising the premium increases perceived gap and conversion on quality-seeking buyers.

user: D2C pet-care brand, ₹7L/mo ads, AOV ₹3,050, GM 44%, ROAS 2.9, CAC ₹1,040, 90-day repeat 19%. Need a step-by-step decision plan for: (a) hire a full-time marketer at ₹1.4L/mo, (b) sign an agency at ₹1L/mo, or (c) keep DIY with one freelance editor. Walk me through how to decide.
assistant:
Run the contribution first because it changes the framing: ₹3,050 × 44% − ₹1,040 = ₹302 per first order. Healthy but not generous. At ₹7L ad spend that's roughly ₹2L of first-order contribution monthly, plus whatever the 19% 90-day repeat adds.

Here's the decision tree, step by step.

1. Eliminate the agency first. ₹1L/month for a ₹7L spend account is the worst zone for agencies — you're not big enough to get a senior strategist (they go to ₹25L+ accounts), so you'll get a 22-year-old account exec running templates. The agency's incentive is to keep your spend stable, not to optimise it. At your scale, agencies underperform a competent freelancer 80% of the time. Cross (b) off.

2. The real choice is between (a) full-time hire at ₹1.4L/mo and (c) DIY + freelancer. The non-obvious test is not "can I afford the hire" — it's "is my CAC and creative cadence at the ceiling of what one founder can produce." Two checks:

 - How many creatives are you shipping per week? If under 4 fresh assets/week, you're capacity-constrained, and a hire pays for itself by breaking that ceiling. If 6+, you're not capacity-constrained, you're optimisation-constrained, and the next 20% improvement isn't a headcount problem.
 - Has CAC improved month-over-month for the last 3 months? If yes, you (or your freelancer) are learning the account. Don't hand it off — a new hire will undo 3 months of learnings while they reorient. If CAC has been flat or rising despite effort, you've hit your skill ceiling.

3. If both checks say "yes, hire," don't hire a generalist marketer at ₹1.4L. Hire a performance marketer specifically, and pay ₹1.1L base + ₹30K performance bonus tied to a specific metric (e.g. blended CAC under ₹900). The structure forces alignment from day one.

4. The non-obvious move: at 19% 90-day repeat, your highest-leverage hire might not be a marketer at all. It's a retention/CRM operator at ₹70-80K/month who lives in Klaviyo and WhatsApp. Moving repeat from 19% to 28% on your current ₹302 first-order contribution is worth ~₹2L/month — more than what a new performance marketer would unlock on acquisition.

Do the two checks in step 2 this week. If the answer is hire, hire retention not paid. That's the one most pet-care brands at your stage get wrong.

ROAS 1.5 at ₹17.5L spend means top-of-funnel is the bleeder — Meta is showing your ads to people who don't recognise themselves in your visuals, so the CTR is okay but conversion lags. That isn't a targeting problem (the algorithm is finding eyewear-interested users), it's a self-identification problem (those users see the ad and don't think the brand is for them). assistant:
You're right, and your team is reasoning from short-term pipeline anxiety. Validate, with one important addition.

The math says you can afford the pause. 560 trials × 14% trial→paid = 78 customers/month × ₹4L ACV = ~₹3.1Cr of new ARR signed monthly. At a 10-week sales cycle, the pipeline you generate today closes in week 10-12, which means your December revenue depends on October's email — pausing 60 days hits February-March revenue, not next month's. Critically, with $50K MRR and 6% monthly churn (~₹2.4L MRR leaking), you have a ~12-week buffer where existing signed deals will keep closing while you rebuild the email engine. The pause window is real.

The deliverability diagnosis is also correct. One domain × 800/day × 8 months is roughly 190K sends from one IP/domain reputation. Even with perfect list hygiene, Google's spam algorithms degrade single-domain reputations past ~120K total sends. You're now landing in promotions or spam on Gmail/Outlook for half your sends — which means even your 4 fresh domains won't fix anything if the underlying playbook is the same.

The non-obvious addition your plan is missing: don't just rebuild domains, rebuild segments. 800/day from one domain to a generalist list is the structural cause. The correct architecture is 4 domains × 50 highly-segmented sends/day each = 200/day total volume but 4x targeting precision. Lower volume, much higher reply rate, vastly better deliverability. Your trial→paid is 14% — solid — which suggests the buyers who DO engage convert well. So volume isn't your friend; precision is. Use the 60-day pause to:

1. Set up 4 fresh domains, warm them properly (30-45 days minimum, ramping from 20/day to 50/day).

2. Re-segment ICPs by company size, HR-tech stack, and trigger event (new HR head, funding round, mass hiring posting). 4 domains = 4 distinct segments with tailored copy each.

3. Run a parallel LinkedIn outbound motion during the pause — 30 personalised messages/day from the founder's account. Won't fully replace 800 cold emails but produces ~10-15 qualified trials/month, enough to keep pipeline from going to zero.

4. Re-launch at ~200/day total at 60 days, scale to 400/day only after deliverability holds.

At 31% 90-day repeat with no incremental CAC, those second orders carry ~₹621 of contribution. The business is healthy enough that attribution is a budget-allocation problem, not an existential one.

Now Triple Whale specifically. It's a useful tool but it is not "source of truth" — it's a model that triangulates Shopify, Meta, and Google data with its own attribution logic, and the logic is opinionated. Treating any third-party attribution tool as ground truth, especially as the basis for pausing campaigns at ROAS 1.5, is how brands kill campaigns that were actually working. The right plan, in order:

If 40% of survey buyers say Instagram and Triple Whale shows Meta at 8% of revenue, you know Triple Whale's wrong, not Meta.

3. Run a holdout test before you trust ANY attribution tool. Pause Meta in one Tier-2 city for 2 weeks; watch revenue in that city. The drop (or lack of it) tells you Meta's true incremental contribution far more honestly than any dashboard. Cost: zero. Insight: priceless.

4. Only after steps 1-3, layer Triple Whale on as a decision-support tool, not a source of truth. ₹15K/mo is fine for that role.

That's the fundamental: matching a price cut doesn't just lower revenue, it lowers the thin slice of margin you actually keep — and at a 30% margin you have the least room of anyone to play this game. The competitor who undercut you is making the same mistake; one of you runs out of cash first.

So it's neither A nor B as you framed them. Hold price, but don't 'risk losing sales' passively — give the buyer a reason the cheaper option can't match. Bundle, a loyalty refill price, faster delivery, a results guarantee on the product itself. Compete on the value around the price, not the price.
